bull_argument.argument:
**The setup: a cash-generative near-monopoly asset trading at a de-rated multiple after a 30% drawdown.** CDB is not a turnaround story or a speculative growth bet — it is a mature Malaysian telecom throwing off a 29.69% operating margin and a 17.4% free cash flow margin, with a 4.69% dividend yield that the fundamentals work explicitly describes as "underpinned by solid fundamentals" rather than balance-sheet stretch. That combination — high margin, high FCF conversion, covered yield — is the definition of an asset you want to own when it goes on sale. And it has gone on sale: the macro report itself concedes a 30% YTD decline. The market has already repriced this name for a hostile rate environment. You are not paying for optimism here; you are being paid 4.69% to wait.

**The valuation math is the core of the bull case.** P/E compresses from 22.23x to 18.28x forward — a ~18% multiple contraction on forward earnings, which means the sell side is modelling real earnings growth ahead, not decay. For a business with these margins, a beta of 0.232, and a covered mid-single-digit yield, 18x forward is undemanding. Note what beta 0.232 actually tells you: this stock has historically decoupled from broad market drawdowns. So the 30% YTD fall is not a beta event — it is a rate-driven multiple compression on a bond-proxy asset. That is precisely the kind of de-rating that reverses mechanically when the discount rate turns. The macro analyst's own diagnosis ("Fed's higher-for-longer stance limits dividend multiple expansion") is an admission that the bear case is a *rates* call, not a *business* call. Rate calls mean-revert; franchise erosion does not. We are being handed the asset at the point of maximum rate pessimism.

**Three of four analysts are constructive, and the fourth is the least durable input.** Fundamentals: buy, *high* confidence — the only high-confidence signal in the entire report set. Sentiment: buy, with an analyst consensus that has been *stable for three months* (57% Buy vs. 14% Sell on the conservative read, 80% bullish on the fundamentals read — either way a 4:1 ratio) and, critically, no deterioration. Macro: neutral, not negative. The single bearish signal is technical, at medium confidence, and its own author admits "neutral RSI prevents high-conviction bearish call." A 6.2% deficit to the SMA-200 with the SMA-50 still holding as support is a stock basing after a de-rating, not one breaking down. Sentiment flags "neither fresh catalysts nor deteriorating sentiment" — I read that as coiled optionality: for a covered 4.69% yielder at 18x forward, you do not need a catalyst to make money, you need the absence of impairment. That is exactly what the data shows.
key_points: **Quality at a discount, not a value trap**: 29.69% operating margin and 17.4% FCF margin fund the 4.69% dividend from cash flow, not leverage — the fundamentals analyst is the only one in the set at *high* confidence, and they say buy.

**Forward P/E of 18.28x vs. trailing 22.23x implies earnings growth ahead**, not decline. An 18% multiple compression on forward estimates is the sell side modelling expansion — you are paying a mature-utility multiple for a business with software-like margins.

**The 30% YTD drawdown is a rate event, not a business event.** With beta at 0.232 this stock does not fall with the market; it fell with the discount rate. The macro report's own wording — 'higher-for-longer *limits dividend multiple expansion*' — concedes the bear case is a rates call that mean-reverts, and it still only rates the name neutral.

**Signal count favours the bulls 3-to-1 on the durable inputs**: buy/high (fundamentals), buy/medium (sentiment), neutral/medium (macro) against a single sell/medium (technical) whose author self-qualifies it as low-conviction given neutral RSI.

**Stable consensus is a feature for an income asset.** 4:1 Buy-to-Sell held flat for three months with no negative news flow means no impairment. bear_argument.argument:
**Start with the arithmetic the bull case never runs: this dividend is not covered.** Yield × P/E = payout ratio. 4.69% × 22.23 = **104% of trailing earnings**. CDB is paying out more than it earns. On the forward number it is still ~86% (4.69% × 18.28). The fundamentals report calls the yield "underpinned by solid fundamentals" — what actually underpins it is a payout ratio with zero headroom, in a capital-intensive industry, funded down to a 17.4% FCF margin that must simultaneously absorb 5G network capex. The bull's core claim — "you are being paid 4.69% to wait" — assumes the coupon is safe. It is the single most fragile line item in the whole file. One weak quarter, one capex step-up, one refinancing at MYR-adjusted rates, and the payout gets rebased. And when a bond proxy cuts its distribution, you do not lose the yield in isolation; you lose the yield *and* the multiple, simultaneously, to the same buyer base that owned it only for the income.

**Second: 22.23x trailing is not a de-rated multiple, it is a premium multiple for a no-growth telecom.** The bull frames the fall from 22.23x to 18.28x as "the sell side modelling real earnings growth ahead." Look at what that actually requires: **21.6% EPS growth** from a mature, ex-growth, single-market Malaysian operator whose own sentiment report describes "no recent news" and "neither fresh catalysts nor deteriorating sentiment." Mature telecoms do not compound earnings at 21%. That forward number is either a normalization assumption, a synergy run-rate already banked, or an estimate that has not yet been cut — and the burden of proof is on the bull to say which. Meanwhile the honest comparison set is regional telecom peers in the low-to-mid teens. Re-rate CDB to 14x forward — a normal multiple for a low-growth, high-payout, FX-exposed operator — and you have **~23% downside from here**, before any dividend action. The stock is not cheap; it is expensive and falling.

**Third: the 30% YTD decline is evidence *against* the bull thesis, not for it.** The bull invokes beta 0.232 to argue this was a rates event, not a business event. That argument inverts itself. A 0.232-beta stock **cannot** lose 30% to market-wide discount-rate moves — that is precisely what low beta means. A 30% drawdown in a 0.23-beta name is, by construction, almost entirely **idiosyncratic**: something specific to this company, this market, or this competitive position. Global bond proxies did not fall 30%. So either beta is meaningless here (in which case stop using it as a safety argument) or the decline is company-specific (in which case the bear case is a business call, not a rates call). You cannot have both. The macro report independently flags the real mechanism: MYR weakness raising USD-denominated capex and debt costs into a capital-intensive rollout — a cash-flow hit, not a valuation artifact. Layer on the technicals — 6.2% below the SMA-200, **failed** rallies off $2.85 support, negative MACD — and the price is telling you the fundamentals report has not marked to market. Note the tell in the sentiment data the bull cited as a strength: consensus has been "stable for three months" at 80% bullish *while the stock fell 30%*. That is not conviction. That is a sell side that has not revised. Stale bullish consensus into a falling price is a downgrade queue, not a support level.

bull_argument.argument:
**The bear's central claim — "this dividend is not covered" — rests on substituting an accounting proxy for the cash test that was actually run.** Yield × P/E is a payout ratio *on reported earnings*, and reported earnings are the single worst denominator you can choose for a post-merger telecom. CDB is CelcomDigi: a combined entity carrying purchase-price amortization on acquired spectrum, licences and customer intangibles — large, non-cash, and mechanically suppressive of reported EPS while leaving cash generation untouched. That is precisely why the file shows a 29.69% operating margin and a 17.4% FCF margin alongside a "104% payout." Both numbers cannot describe a company in distribution stress; one of them is an artifact. And note who ran the cash test: the fundamentals analyst is the only one of four with **high confidence**, the only one who examined the actual financials rather than price action or macro narrative, and the explicit conclusion was that the yield is "underpinned by solid fundamentals." The bear is not correcting that analyst with new data — the bear is overruling a direct reading of the cash flows with a two-variable multiplication. Notice also what the same amortization roll-off plus contracted merger synergies does to the bear's second objection: 22.23x → 18.28x does **not** require "21.6% organic EPS growth" from an ex-growth operator. It requires the integration cost base to normalize and non-cash charges to step down — cost-side, already-identified, largely contractual. The bear demanded the bull name which of the three explanations applies. That is the answer, and it is the least demand-dependent of the three.

**On beta, the bear's inversion argument cuts the wrong way.** Yes — a 0.232-beta name losing 30% means the move was idiosyncratic. Idiosyncratic is not a synonym for *impaired*. There is a third channel the bear skips: ownership and flow. A Malaysian bond-proxy yielder is held by foreign income funds; MYR weakness against a higher-for-longer Fed triggers foreign outflow from exactly that holder base, and the selling is indiscriminate with respect to operating performance. The falsifiable test is simple — if the 30% decline were a business event, it would show up in the operating data. It does not. The 29.69% operating margin and 17.4% FCF margin are **reported actuals, not forecasts**. Price fell 30%; margins did not move. On FX specifically, the bear's "cash-flow hit" is overstated in direction: CDB earns MYR, holds a domestic subscriber base, and pays its dividend in MYR. MYR weakness is a *translation* issue for foreign holders and an input-cost issue on the imported-equipment share of capex — a finite line item — not a revenue or solvency channel. And in Malaysia, 5G access runs through a shared wholesale arrangement rather than duplicated per-operator builds, which is why the capex-crush narrative has not shown up in the margin line the bear must explain away.

**Finally, run the bear's own downside case and look at what it implies.** Re-rate to 14x forward and you get ~23% downside — at which point this asset yields **6.1%** on a 29.69% operating margin, in a consolidated market, with domestic pension capital (EPF and peers) structurally hunting duration-like MYR income. That is a bid, not a void. Meanwhile the bear's "stale bullish consensus is a downgrade queue" gets the sequence backwards: sell-side analysts cut *fastest* into drawdowns, and this consensus has been stable at roughly 4:1 bullish for three months **after** the decline, with sell ratings pinned at 14%. Three months of stability post-fall is the signature of estimates that have already been revised and held, not of a queue about to break. The asymmetry is what closes the case: downside is a multiple already 30% de-rated compressing further on a rates call that mean-reverts; upside is multiple recovery *plus* MYR normalization *plus* synergy delivery, with 4.69% clipped annually while waiting. The only bearish signal in the entire report set is a medium-confidence technical read whose own author wrote that "neutral RSI prevents high-conviction bearish call," with the SMA-50 still functioning as support.

**The bull's rescue of the dividend destroys the bull's valuation case — the two arguments cannot both stand.** To defend a 104% trailing payout, the bull invokes purchase-price amortization on acquired spectrum, licences and customer intangibles: large, non-cash, mechanically suppressing reported EPS. Amortization roll-off does not generate one additional sen of distributable cash flow. So the bull is simultaneously arguing (a) ignore reported earnings, look at cash — and (b) the stock is getting cheaper because reported earnings are about to rise for non-cash reasons. Pick one. If the earnings recovery is non-cash, 18.28x forward is the *identical* cash-flow stream wearing a better denominator, and the correct cash test is the only one that matters — and it is far tighter than the bull admits. Run it: market cap 33.9bn at 22.23x implies net income ~1.53bn; the 4.69% yield is ~1.59bn of cash out the door. The bull's own preferred metric, the 17.4% FCF margin, on a revenue base consistent with a 29.69% operating margin and that net income, puts free cash flow around 2.2–2.3bn. The dividend consumes roughly 70% of *post-capex* free cash flow, leaving well under 1bn of annual retained cash to fund network investment, debt amortization and any working-capital swing. That is not "underpinned by solid fundamentals." That is a company distributing nearly everything it generates, in the most capital-intensive industry in the index, with FX-inflated equipment costs — and it is the entire reason a 4.69% yield exists at a 22x multiple rather than a 15x one.

**The bull's factual foundation is imported from outside the report set, and where it is checkable it is wrong or contradicted.** Nothing in the four analyst reports mentions purchase-price amortization, contracted merger synergies, or a shared 5G wholesale arrangement. Those are the load-bearing beams of the entire round-2 bull case and none of them appear in the evidence file — while the claim that Malaysia avoids "duplicated per-operator builds" is precisely what changed when the single-wholesale-network model gave way to a second 5G network operator, adding both a capex obligation and a price-competitive entrant to a market the bull describes as "consolidated." The bull quoted both figures interchangeably and called it "either way a 4:1 ratio." It is not; and the fact that our only *high-confidence* report appears to have mis-read the consensus table is a reason to discount that report, not to elevate it above the arithmetic. On stickiness: the claim that "sell-side analysts cut fastest into drawdowns" is the opposite of how estimate revisions behave. Three months of frozen bullish ratings *through* a 30% decline is not confirmation; it is the un-revised state that precedes a downgrade cluster.

**The bull has now conceded the decline is idiosyncratic, and that concession is fatal to the only reason to own this stock.** The flow explanation — foreign income funds exiting an MYR bond proxy — does not make the de-rating self-reversing; it makes recovery contingent on the Fed and the ringgit turning, which is an unhedged macro bet on the exact conditions the macro analyst flagged as headwinds at neutral. And "margins didn't move, so nothing is wrong" mistakes a lagging indicator for a leading one: trailing operating margin is the last thing to break, which is why price, not margin, is the early signal — 6.2% below the SMA-200, *failed* rallies off $2.85, negative MACD. More importantly, a 0.232-beta asset that just delivered a 30% single-name drawdown has invalidated its own risk model. Its realized volatility is nothing like a bond proxy's, so it cannot be sized as one — which eliminates the defensive-income sleeve that is the sole legitimate use case here. Now price the asymmetry honestly. The upside is conjunctive: multiple re-rating **and** MYR normalization **and** synergy delivery **and** the payout holding — four independent conditions, and failure of any one caps the return. The downside needs only one. Re-rate to a peer-normal 14x forward and that is ~23% down; if the payout is rebased 25–30% to restore coverage, the "6.1% yield floor" the bull offers as a bid re-prices with it, compounding toward 35–40%. And a yield that rises purely because the price fell against a >100% earnings payout is a distress signal, not a valuation floor — the same "domestic pension bid" logic supported every European telecom in the 2010s right up to each dividend cut. Against that: reverting to 22.23x is +21% plus the coupon, call it ~26%. That is a symmetric-at-best payoff on a stock in a confirmed downtrend, with two buys, one sell and one neutral — no signal convergence, and the single high-confidence buy resting on a coverage claim that does not survive contact with the cash. You do not need to be a permanent bear on Malaysian telecom to conclude the correct action today is no position.

And the bear cannot invoke that mechanism to explain the 22.23x/18.28x gap while insisting the same gap requires 21.6% organic growth from an ex-growth telecom. The consensus discrepancy the bear leans on cuts the same way: 57% buy, 29% hold, **14% sell**. One analyst in seven is negative after a 30% decline. Calling 29% holds "a sell-side euphemism" and three months of stability "a downgrade queue" is a forecast, not evidence; the evidence is that estimates were revised and *held* through the drawdown. On beta: a 0.232 beta and a 30% idiosyncratic drawdown are not in contradiction — low beta *means* low co-movement with the index, so a large single-name move is exactly what the coefficient permits. Idiosyncratic is not a synonym for impaired, and the falsification test is available in the file: if this were a business event, it would appear in the operating data. Margins are reported actuals. Price fell 30%; margins did not move.

**Price the asymmetry with the bear's dividend-cut leg removed, because its own cash math removed it.** The bear's -35% to -40% scenario is the product of two events: a re-rate to an unsourced 14x *and* a payout rebase that 1.4x cash coverage does not support. Take the cut out and the residual downside is a multiple call on a stock already 30% de-rated, in which case you are holding a 4.69% coupon — rising toward 6% on any further weakness — against a domestic MYR income bid, while the two headwinds the macro analyst named (Fed higher-for-longer, MYR weakness) are both mean-reverting rate variables rather than franchise variables, and that analyst rated them **neutral**, not negative. The upside is not as conjunctive as the bear claims: multiple recovery alone to 22.23x is roughly +21% plus the coupon, ~26% total, and it requires nothing from MYR or synergies. MYR normalization and cost normalization are free options layered on top, not preconditions. So the trade is: a documented 1.4x-covered mid-single-digit yield, 29.69% operating margins, 18.28x forward, beta 0.232, three of four signals constructive, bought after the de-rating rather than before it — against a bear case that needs an unsourced peer multiple and a dividend cut its own arithmetic contradicts. The correct action is not the bear's "no position." It is a position sized for a defensive income sleeve, with the drawdown already taken by someone else and the coupon paying you to be patient. The technical damage argues for staging entry, not for standing aside — which is the difference between managing the one bearish signal in the file and pretending it outweighs the other three.

It then charged that same free cash flow a second time for network capex, when a 17.4% FCF margin is post-capex by definition. Remove the double count and the bear's own arithmetic vindicates the high-confidence fundamentals report it set out to discredit. The "pick one" dilemma between the cash defense and the valuation case is likewise false — cash flow determines coupon survival, reported EPS determines the multiple, and an amortization roll-off legitimately moves the second without moving the first. On evidence, the bear's objection to facts "imported from outside the report set" applies with equal force to its own 14x peer multiple, its hypothetical 25–30% payout rebase, and its second-network entrant, none of which appear in the file — and its entire -35% to -40% tail depends on the cut leg its own cash math just eliminated. On beta, a 0.232 coefficient measures co-movement with the index, so a large single-name drawdown is permitted, not disqualifying; and the bear never explains why a supposed business impairment left a 29.69% operating margin and 17.4% FCF margin — both reported actuals — entirely intact. Finally, "stale consensus is a downgrade queue" is a prediction dressed as evidence; the evidence is 14% sell ratings held stable for three months *after* the decline.

bear_argument.argument:
**The bull's "1.4x covered" is the amortization argument eating itself.** I'll concede the narrow point: a 17.4% FCF margin is post-capex, and charging routine network capex against it twice was wrong. But look at what the bull has to believe to get to 1.4x. The gap between ~1.53bn of net income and ~2.2–2.3bn of free cash flow is, on the bull's own account, the purchase-price amortization of *spectrum, licences and customer intangibles*. The bull wants that charge treated as fictional when defending the coupon — and then treated as real enough to roll off and re-rate the stock. It is neither. For a telecom, amortized spectrum is deferred cash: licences expire and get re-auctioned, and that outlay lands as a lumpy cash event that no single year's capex line contains. So the "1.4x" is coverage measured against a cash flow that is flattered by exactly the obligation the bull has defined away. Strip the accounting fight out entirely and the undisputed facts are these: the company distributes ~70% of post-capex free cash flow and more than 100% of reported earnings, retaining ~650m a year against 5G-era investment, debt amortization, FX-inflated imported equipment and eventual spectrum renewal, in a 33.9bn-cap capital-intensive business. That is a payout with no error budget. It is not a lie; it is simply not the "solid fundamentals" underpinning the bull needs it to be, and it is why the market prices a 4.69% yield here rather than 3%.

**On evidence discipline, the tu quoque fails, and the one internal contradiction in the file is in the bull's key document.** The bull answers "your merger-synergy, wholesale-5G and PPA claims aren't in the reports" with "your 14x isn't either." The difference is function. My 14x is a labelled scenario input for pricing downside; the bull's imported facts are *load-bearing* — remove PPA amortization and the coverage defence collapses, remove contracted synergies and the 22.23x→18.28x compression reverts to requiring ~21.6% EPS growth from an operator the sentiment report describes as having no catalysts and no news. A scenario you can reject and still hold my conclusion; a premise you reject and the bull's conclusion is gone. Meanwhile the only contradiction I raised that is entirely *inside* the file remains unanswered: the fundamentals report says "80% bullish consensus," the sentiment report reads the same table as 57% buy / 29% hold / 14% sell. The bull's response was to quietly adopt the sentiment numbers and re-describe them as strength. Fine — then the single high-confidence buy signal in this report set contains a demonstrable misreading of its own inputs, and high confidence is a claim about the analyst, not about the company. Note also the structural read the bull never disputes: two buys, one neutral, one sell is *low signal convergence*, which in this framework is the definition of a low-conviction file. And the bull's own closing recommends "staging entry" because of the technical damage. That is a concession that today is not the entry point — which is my conclusion wearing a longer time horizon.

**Price it against the alternative, and the trade has no edge.** You are being offered ~4.69% in ringgit, from an equity paying out nearly everything it earns, in a single emerging market, with a stock 6.2% below its 200-day, failing at $2.85, on negative MACD, into a Fed the macro analyst explicitly flags as higher-for-longer. The risk-free rate that same Fed stance implies sits close enough to that coupon that the entire equity risk premium here — single-country regulatory risk, competitive risk, FX translation risk, payout risk, a demonstrated 30% single-name drawdown — is being compensated by roughly nothing. The bull's upside is "revert to 22.23x, +21% plus coupon," which is pure circularity: it assumes the de-rating was a mistake, in a name whose 0.232 beta means the market cannot have made that mistake for macro reasons — it was idiosyncratic, and 0.232 therefore cannot also be offered as a defensiveness credential in the closing summary. You cannot size this into a bond-proxy income sleeve on a coefficient that just failed by 30%. The downside needs only one thing to go wrong; the upside needs the multiple call *and* no payout rebase *and* the MYR to stop deteriorating. The correct action is no new position. If you already own it, do not add, and do not let a 4.69% coupon talk you out of noticing that the price, the payout ratio and the currency are all telling the same story.

I concede the double-count on capex — but the bull cannot claim the net-income-to-FCF gap is non-cash amortization of spectrum and licences while treating the resulting FCF as durable distributable cash; expiring spectrum is deferred cash outlay, so the coverage ratio is measured against a flattered denominator. bull_case_summary: CDB (CelcomDigi) is a mature, cash-generative Malaysian telecom with 29.69% operating margins and a 17.4% post-capex FCF margin, now on sale after a ~30% YTD de-rating. At 22.23x trailing / 18.28x forward with a 4.69% yield, the bull argues you are paid to wait for a rate-driven multiple compression to mean-revert. Key rebuttals: the "104% payout" is an artifact of reported EPS depressed by post-merger purchase-price amortization on spectrum/licences/intangibles — on the bear's own cash figures (net income ~1.53bn, dividend ~1.59bn, FCF ~2.2–2.3bn) the dividend is ~1.4x covered by free cash flow, and the bear double-counted capex already deducted in the FCF margin. The forward multiple compression therefore needs cost/non-cash normalization, not 21.6% organic EPS growth. The 30% fall is idiosyncratic but flow-driven (foreign income funds exiting an MYR bond proxy), not operational — margins are reported actuals and did not move. Three of four signals are constructive, including the only high-confidence one; the sole bearish signal is a medium-confidence technical read whose author disclaims high conviction. Recommendation: own it as a defensive income position, staging entry to respect the technical damage; multiple recovery alone is ~+21% plus coupon, with MYR and synergy upside as free options.
bear_case_summary: The only reason to own CDB is the coupon, and the coupon has no error budget. On reported earnings the payout exceeds 100% (4.69% × 22.23); even granting the FCF correction, the company distributes ~70% of post-capex free cash flow, retaining only ~650m a year against 5G investment, debt amortization, FX-inflated imported equipment and eventual spectrum re-auction — and amortized spectrum is deferred cash, so the FCF "coverage" is flattered by the very charge the bull defines away. The bull's amortization defence is self-cancelling: if the forward earnings recovery is non-cash, 18.28x forward is the same cash stream with a better denominator. 22.23x is a premium, not de-rated, multiple for a no-growth single-market operator; re-rating to a peer-normal 14x forward is ~23% downside, and a 25–30% payout rebase compounds toward 35–40%. A 0.232-beta stock that fell 30% has invalidated its own risk model, so it cannot be sized into a defensive-income sleeve — and the same low beta means the decline was idiosyncratic, not a reversible macro mistake. The bull's load-bearing facts (PPA, contracted synergies, shared 5G wholesale) come from outside the report set, and the sole high-confidence report misreads its own consensus table ("80% bullish" vs. 57/29/14). With two buys, one neutral, one sell there is no signal convergence, the coupon barely exceeds the implied risk-free rate, and the bull's own "stage entry" concedes today is not the entry. Correct action: no new position; if held, do not add.
key_points_of_agreement: The ~30% YTD drawdown in a 0.232-beta name is idiosyncratic rather than a broad-market beta event (the bull conceded this explicitly).
The 17.4% FCF margin is post-capex, so charging routine network capex against it a second time was an error (the bear conceded this).

On cash terms the dividend consumes roughly 70% of post-capex free cash flow — both sides ultimately work from the same ~1.53bn net income / ~1.59bn dividend / ~2.2–2.3bn FCF figures; they disagree only on whether that is comfort or fragility.
Operating performance in the file shows no deterioration: 29.69% operating margin and 17.4% FCF margin are reported actuals that did not move with the price.
The macro backdrop (higher-for-longer Fed, MYR weakness) is a genuine headwind for an MYR bond-proxy yielder.
The technical picture is negative — 6.2% below SMA-200, failed rallies off $2.85, negative MACD — and argues against buying aggressively today (bull: stage entry; bear: no position).
There is no fresh catalyst and no recent news; this is a mature, low-growth business.
The fundamentals report's "80% bullish consensus" does not reconcile with the sentiment report's 57% buy / 29% hold / 14% sell reading of the same table.
key_points_of_disagreement: Dividend safety: bull says ~1.4x FCF coverage with ~650m retained is normal infrastructure-asset behaviour; bear says >100% earnings payout plus deferred spectrum cash leaves zero error budget and is why the yield is 4.69% and not 3%.

Whether the amortization argument is coherent: bull separates cash (coupon survival) from reported EPS (multiple applied); bear says you cannot call the charge fictional for coverage and real-enough-to-roll-off for re-rating.
What the 22.23x→18.28x compression implies: cost/non-cash normalization (bull) vs. an unrevised or unachievable ~21.6% EPS growth assumption (bear).
Whether 22.23x is a de-rated multiple or still a premium one for a no-growth telecom; and whether 14x peer-normal is the right anchor.
Reversibility of the de-rating: mean-reverting rate/flow event (bull) vs. company- and market-specific impairment plus an unhedged Fed/MYR bet (bear).
Whether beta 0.232 still qualifies the stock for a defensive-income sleeve after a 30% single-name drawdown.
Interpretation of three months of stable bullish consensus through the decline: estimates already revised and held (bull) vs. an un-revised downgrade queue (bear).
Evidence discipline: bull calls the bear's 14x and payout-cut scenarios equally unsourced; bear distinguishes labelled scenario inputs from load-bearing premises imported from outside the file.

Whether the FX channel is a finite imported-capex cost and translation issue (bull) or a real cash-flow and solvency-adjacent hit (bear).

Whether purchase-price amortization on merger intangibles genuinely explains the earnings/FCF gap, and how large it is — asserted by the bull, absent from the report set.
Timing and magnitude of spectrum licence renewal / re-auction cash outlays, which sit outside any single year's capex line.

The current structure of Malaysia's 5G rollout (single shared wholesale network vs. a second network operator) and its capex and price-competition implications.
The true sell-side consensus — the two reports contradict each other, and whether the high-confidence fundamentals report misread its own table is undetermined.
The cause of the 30% idiosyncratic drawdown: foreign-holder outflow, regulatory/competitive news, or something not captured in the four reports.
Trajectory of MYR and Fed policy, on which the bull's multiple-recovery thesis depends.
The appropriate peer multiple for a high-payout, single-market, FX-exposed operator (the 14x anchor is unsourced).
Whether the current level marks a base after de-rating or a continuation of a downtrend — the technical evidence is genuinely two-sided (SMA-50 support vs. failed rallies and negative MACD).
Malaysian regulatory and competitive risk, including tariff pressure and any state or pension-fund ownership dynamics that could support or constrain the payout.
